video_title: AI Is Upending the Lives of People Who Do Social Media Professionally | Odd Lots
gist: Recorded live in LA, Tracy Alloway and Joe Weisenthal talk to Taylor Lorenz (User Mag) and Rachel Karten (Link In Bio) about how AI is changing the creator economy and social-media work. They say AI is being pushed on marketing teams from the top and without training. How-to creators are the most exposed, and AI slop is gaming Instagram in the short term. Meta looks like a 2010s-era 'dinosaur' next to Google, and the creators still winning make serialized, show-like content.

themes.theme: Top-down AI mandates on marketing teams

insights.claim: Social-media consultant Rachel Karten, after talking to roughly 100 marketers, says AI mostly reaches marketing teams through bosses who push it on staff and use it to replace their own judgment. Examples include running a social manager's meme through Claude to ask whether it is funny, and approving only ideas that appear to come from Copilot.
insights.speaker: Rachel Karten
insights.so_what: Enterprise AI-seat adoption in marketing is being driven by managers rather than practitioners, so usage numbers may overstate real productivity gains and hide falling morale.
insights.quote: they're outsourcing all of their gut instincts to AI

insights.claim: According to Rachel Karten, AI is being rolled out on marketing teams as an untrained free-for-all. Earlier enterprise software, such as the project tool Condé Nast adopted (transcribed as 'a sauna', likely Asana), came with months of workflow onboarding.
insights.speaker: Rachel Karten
insights.so_what: Missing training and workflow design is a bottleneck to AI ROI in creative functions and an opening for AI-enablement and training vendors.

insights.claim: Marketers are generally not succeeding at using generative AI to write captions or post ideas. The productive use Rachel Karten sees is agencies mocking up big real-world ideas in pitch decks so that clients who lack imagination can picture them.
insights.speaker: Rachel Karten
insights.so_what: AI's near-term marketing value is in visualizing ideas and selling them to clients, not in replacing copywriting. That tempers bull cases built on AI-generated social content at scale.
insights.quote: I don't hear that a lot of marketers are having success having it generate captions or post ideas

insights.claim: Tech journalist Taylor Lorenz uses AI only as an assistive tool, for SEO captions and resizing images in Canva, not for writing. She says current AI editing tools cannot even edit a podcast.
insights.speaker: Taylor Lorenz
insights.so_what: AI video and audio editing tools still fall short of professional creators' needs, so the creator-tooling market remains open.
insights.quote: It cannot even edit a podcast.

themes.theme: Brand trust vs. consumer appetite for AI content

insights.claim: Consumers read AI-generated brand content as a shortcut that suggests the company also cuts corners on its product. Rachel Karten argues that brands like Nike built their identity on visible investment in creative work.
insights.speaker: Rachel Karten
insights.so_what: Brands that swap human creative work for AI imagery risk brand equity. Visible creative craft may become a differentiator and a reason for premium pricing.

insights.claim: Audiences often enjoy AI-generated content, including YouTubers reading AI-written scripts that commenters praise, as long as they don't feel deceived. Taylor Lorenz says the backlash is about feeling tricked, not about AI itself.
insights.speaker: Taylor Lorenz
insights.so_what: Disclosure and authenticity norms, rather than AI use itself, will decide whether AI content monetizes. Platforms' labeling policies are the lever to watch.
insights.quote: I think people just don't want to feel tricked.

insights.claim: The same consumers who attack a company for an AI-generated menu happily share AI 'fruit slop' memes like 'Fruit Love Island'. People accept AI in low-stakes meme culture but expect craft from companies they buy from.
insights.speaker: Rachel Karten
insights.so_what: AI content succeeds in entertainment and meme niches and faces pushback in commercial brand communications, so expect different adoption curves by use case.

insights.claim: Creators who built audiences on how-to content (makeup tutorials, home repair) are the most exposed to AI. People will ask chatbots how to fix a dishwasher instead, as Taylor Lorenz's mother did when she used ChatGPT to fix a toilet.
insights.speaker: Taylor Lorenz
insights.so_what: Instructional and search-style creator content, and the ad and affiliate revenue it earns, is the part of the creator economy most at risk of moving to AI assistants.
insights.quote: And I actually think AI is a better authority when people will turn to AI for how to fix their dishwasher.

insights.claim: Creators whose value comes from parasocial connection, personal opinion or commentary that is hard to copy are better placed. They can use AI tools to make better content while their output stays hard to replicate.
insights.speaker: Taylor Lorenz
insights.so_what: Durable creator economics shift toward personality- and opinion-driven formats, which supports platforms and tools built around parasocial fan relationships.

insights.claim: The accounts growing fastest in 2026 run serialized, TV-show-like formats with a recurring through line. One example is a restaurant cook who records his cooking with Meta glasses and reportedly reached about 500,000 followers in 2-3 months. Lifestyle 'share my life' influencing is declining and draws anger.
insights.speaker: Rachel Karten / Taylor Lorenz
insights.so_what: Creator value is moving to episodic entertainment IP, which favors creators and platforms that monetize like TV. Lifestyle-influencer ad budgets may be exposed.
insights.quote: so don't try to be a lifestyle influencer in 2026.

insights.claim: Talent agencies are building AI likeness vaults. The transcript names 'Sia' and a 'CIA vault', probably an auto-caption of CAA. In this model a star or influencer shows up for a single day of capture, and AI then retouches and tailors the output for different audiences. Taylor Lorenz expects this to become the standard model.
insights.speaker: Taylor Lorenz
insights.so_what: Licensing talent likenesses creates a new revenue line for agencies and cuts production costs, a trend relevant to agency, ad-production and AI-video businesses.

insights.claim: AI accounts that post around 50 times a day are 'pulling the slot machine' of Instagram's algorithm. Rachel Karten found that 2 or 3 of the top 20 most-viewed Reels ever are recent AI-generated videos, some built to confuse viewers about what is real.
insights.speaker: Rachel Karten
insights.so_what: AI volume is gaming engagement metrics now, which boosts short-term engagement but risks long-term platform trust and advertiser quality. Watch for Meta policy changes on AI content.
insights.quote: I think that's a short term benefit for really bad long term results.

insights.claim: Taylor Lorenz argues that social platforms are on the back foot in the AI transition. She sees Meta as a 2010s-era 'dinosaur' whose influence peaked in that decade, and Google as better positioned.
insights.speaker: Taylor Lorenz
insights.so_what: Sentiment is a relative negative for META against GOOGL in the AI-era attention contest, though this comes from a journalist's cultural read, not financial analysis.
insights.quote: Google is better position than meta. Meta is in a really hard place right now

insights.claim: Under Instagram's own format guidance, carousels and Reels reach non-followers, and non-follower views now fuel the algorithm. Single-image posts serve existing followers, and Stories and DMs are where community happens. Adam Mosseri has said the 'social' in social media is now DMing friends things that remind you of them.
insights.speaker: Rachel Karten
insights.so_what: Social activity is moving from public feeds into private messaging, which pushes Meta's monetization toward discovery Reels and messaging surfaces.

insights.claim: One of the guests called Meta's Threads the most toxic social platform. Its algorithm favors angry replies and produces fast pile-ons, and its AI-generated news summaries sometimes make things up.
insights.speaker: guest (Rachel Karten or Taylor Lorenz)
insights.so_what: Threads may have weak brand safety and advertiser appeal, which matters for Meta's hopes of monetizing it.

insights.claim: Joe Weisenthal suggests chatbot time may pull attention away from social scrolling, because conversations with Claude or ChatGPT are pleasant and never insult the user the way social comment sections do.
insights.speaker: Joe Weisenthal
insights.so_what: If chat assistants take share of daily attention, social platforms' ad inventory and engagement growth could face a new structural competitor.

insights.claim: Taylor Lorenz predicts the smartphone form factor will die soon as wearables, earbuds, AI pins you whisper to, smart glasses and smart home devices move interaction toward ambient computing. Rachel Karten disagrees and says she doesn't see that happening in the real world.
insights.speaker: Taylor Lorenz
insights.so_what: A move from screens to ambient AI would change how feed-based ad platforms monetize. The guests disagree, so treat this as a thesis to watch, not consensus.
insights.quote: I do think that, like this form factor of this type of phone is going to die quite soon.

insights.claim: Public opposition to data centers is a 2026 midterm election-cycle issue rather than a 2028 one, a view Taylor Lorenz credits to a political consultant. Data-center opponents and AI-doom critics have not formed a coherent coalition.
insights.speaker: Taylor Lorenz
insights.so_what: Near-term political and local permitting risk for data-center buildouts is concentrated around the 2026 cycle, while the fragmented anti-AI opposition limits wider regulatory momentum.
insights.quote: It's actually a very 2026 election cycle issue

insights.claim: Taylor Lorenz argues that anthropomorphizing AI distorts policy debates about liability, because AI products are computer programs, not living beings with agency.
insights.speaker: Taylor Lorenz
insights.so_what: How lawmakers frame AI agency will shape who bears liability, the model makers or the deployers, which matters for AI companies' legal exposure.
